title: Anatomy & Physiology II
summary: The second semester of college A&P in syllabus order: endocrine, blood, heart, vessels, lymphatic and immune, respiratory, digestive, metabolism, urinary, and reproduction with development. Built around the mechanisms lecture exams ask you to explain and the structures the lab practical asks you to name.

lessons.title: The endocrine system: glands, hormones, and axes
lessons.body:
The nervous system sends fast, targeted, short-lived messages down wires. The endocrine system sends slow, broadcast, long-lasting messages through blood. Only cells with the matching **receptor** respond, which is how a hormone in every vessel acts on only a few tissues.

## Hormone classes and mechanisms

**Water-soluble hormones** — all peptides and proteins plus the catecholamines — cannot cross the membrane. They bind a surface receptor and use a **second messenger**, usually cyclic AMP through a G protein, to activate enzymes already in the cell. Fast onset, short duration.

**Lipid-soluble hormones** — steroids from cholesterol (cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, testosterone) and thyroid hormone — diffuse through the membrane, bind an intracellular receptor, and act directly on DNA to turn genes on or off. Slow onset (hours), long duration. They travel bound to carrier proteins.

> **Key:** Second messenger equals fast and reversible. Gene transcription equals slow and sustained. Every timing question on the exam comes back to that split.

Release is triggered three ways: **humoral** (a blood level, like calcium driving PTH), **neural** (a nerve, like sympathetic fibers driving the adrenal medulla), and **hormonal** (a hormone driving a hormone, the tropic pattern).

## The pituitary and its axes

The **hypothalamus** controls the **anterior pituitary** through releasing and inhibiting hormones sent down a private portal blood system. The anterior pituitary then makes six: **GH**, **TSH**, **ACTH**, **FSH**, **LH**, **prolactin**.

The **posterior pituitary** is not a gland at all — it is nerve endings that store and release two hypothalamic hormones: **ADH (vasopressin)**, which makes the collecting duct reabsorb water, and **oxytocin**, for uterine contraction and milk ejection.

The classic axes run on **negative feedback**: hypothalamus to pituitary to target gland, with the final hormone shutting off the first two. Thyroid: TRH to TSH to `T3`/`T4`. Adrenal cortex: CRH to ACTH to cortisol. Gonads: GnRH to FSH and LH to estrogen or testosterone.

## The major glands

| Gland | Hormone | Main action |
|---|---|---|
| Thyroid follicles | `T3`, `T4` | Raise basal metabolic rate; need iodine |
| Thyroid C cells | Calcitonin | Lowers blood calcium |
| Parathyroid | PTH | Raises blood calcium |
| Adrenal cortex, zona glomerulosa | Aldosterone | Retain sodium and water, excrete potassium |
| Adrenal cortex, zona fasciculata | Cortisol | Raise glucose, suppress inflammation, stress response |
| Adrenal medulla | Epinephrine, norepinephrine | Sympathetic surge |
| Pancreas, beta cells | Insulin | Lowers blood glucose |
| Pancreas, alpha cells | Glucagon | Raises blood glucose |
| Pineal | Melatonin | Sleep-wake rhythm |
| Thymus | Thymosin | T-lymphocyte maturation |

## Glucose control, the exam favorite

Fasting glucose is normally `70–99 mg/dL`. After a meal, beta cells release **insulin**, which moves `GLUT4` transporters into muscle and fat membranes, drives glycogenesis and lipogenesis, and lowers blood glucose. Between meals, alpha cells release **glucagon**, which drives **glycogenolysis** and **gluconeogenesis** in the liver and raises it. Cortisol, growth hormone, and epinephrine all raise it too.

## Disorders worth knowing

- **Type 1 diabetes**: autoimmune loss of beta cells, no insulin. **Type 2**: insulin resistance. Both give the three P's — polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia — because glucose above the renal threshold of about `180 mg/dL` drags water into the urine.
- **Hyperthyroidism (Graves)**: weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia, exophthalmos. **Hypothyroidism**: weight gain, cold intolerance, fatigue; iodine deficiency causes goiter.
- **Cushing syndrome**: excess cortisol — moon face, central obesity, thin skin, hyperglycemia. **Addison disease**: adrenal insufficiency — hypotension, hyperkalemia, bronzed skin.
- **Acromegaly** is excess GH after the growth plates close; **gigantism** is excess GH before.
- **Diabetes insipidus** is too little ADH: enormous volumes of dilute urine with normal glucose.

> **Trap:** Diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus share a name and nothing else. Mellitus is a glucose problem; insipidus is a water problem.
keyPoints: Water-soluble hormones use surface receptors and second messengers; lipid-soluble hormones enter the cell and change gene transcription.
The anterior pituitary makes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin; the posterior pituitary only stores ADH and oxytocin.
Endocrine axes run on negative feedback from the target hormone back to hypothalamus and pituitary.
Insulin lowers glucose via GLUT4, glycogenesis and lipogenesis; glucagon raises it via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Aldosterone retains sodium and water and excretes potassium; cortisol raises glucose and suppresses inflammation.

checks.q: A hormone binds a receptor inside the cell nucleus and changes which genes are transcribed. It is most likely:
choices: A peptide hormone such as insulin
A steroid hormone such as cortisol
checks.why: Only lipid-soluble hormones (steroids and thyroid hormone) cross the membrane to reach intracellular receptors. Insulin and epinephrine are water-soluble and act through second messengers at the surface.

checks.q: A patient has high TSH and low T4. The most likely problem is:
checks.why: A failing thyroid cannot make T4, so negative feedback is lost and TSH climbs. Pituitary failure would give low TSH with low T4.

checks.q: Which combination correctly pairs hormone and effect?
choices: ADH: increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct
checks.why: ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct to conserve water. Aldosterone retains sodium and excretes potassium, glucagon raises glucose, and calcitonin lowers calcium.

lessons.title: Blood: composition, hematopoiesis, hemostasis, and typing
lessons.body:
Blood is a connective tissue with a liquid matrix. Adult volume is about `5 L`, pH `7.35–7.45`, temperature `38 C`, and it is about `8%` of body weight.

## Composition

Spin it in a tube and it separates: **plasma** on top (about `55%`), a thin buffy coat of white cells and platelets, and **erythrocytes** on the bottom. The red cell fraction is the **hematocrit** — roughly `42–52%` in men and `37–47%` in women.

Plasma is about `92%` water. The plasma proteins are **albumin** (most abundant; the main source of colloid osmotic pressure that holds water in vessels), **globulins** (transport and antibodies), and **fibrinogen** (clotting). Serum is plasma with the clotting factors removed.

## Red blood cells

Biconcave discs, no nucleus and no mitochondria — which maximizes hemoglobin space and means an RBC cannot consume the oxygen it carries. Each cell holds about `250 million` hemoglobin molecules; each hemoglobin has four heme groups with iron, so one molecule carries four `O2`. Normal hemoglobin is about `13.5–17.5 g/dL` in men and `12–16 g/dL` in women. Lifespan is about `120` days, ending in the spleen and liver, where heme becomes bilirubin (excreted in bile) and iron is recycled.

**Hematopoiesis** starts with the hemocytoblast in red bone marrow. **Erythropoietin (EPO)** from the kidney rises when tissue oxygen falls and drives erythropoiesis — a classic negative feedback loop, and the reason kidney failure causes anemia and altitude causes a rising hematocrit.

## White blood cells

Normal count `4,500–11,000/microliter`. Remember them by abundance: **Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas** — Neutrophils `60–70%`, Lymphocytes `20–25%`, Monocytes `3–8%`, Eosinophils `2–4%`, Basophils under `1%`.

Granulocytes are neutrophils (first responder phagocytes, bacterial infection), eosinophils (parasites and allergy), basophils (release histamine and heparin). Agranulocytes are lymphocytes (B, T, NK — the adaptive response) and monocytes (become macrophages in tissue).

## Hemostasis

Three steps.

1. **Vascular spasm**: injured smooth muscle constricts.
2. **Platelet plug**: platelets stick to exposed collagen, activate, and release ADP and thromboxane A2 to recruit more — positive feedback.
3. **Coagulation**: a cascade converting **prothrombin to thrombin**, then **fibrinogen to fibrin**, which meshes the plug. The **intrinsic pathway** starts with damaged vessel surface, the **extrinsic pathway** with tissue factor from injured tissue; both converge on the common pathway at factor X.

Calcium (factor IV) and vitamin K-dependent factors are required, which is why warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, anticoagulates. Clot retraction pulls edges together; **fibrinolysis** by plasmin dissolves the clot later. Normal platelet count is `150,000–450,000/microliter`.

> **Trap:** A thrombus is a clot formed in place; an embolus is one that broke loose and traveled. The word changes when it moves.

## Blood types

Type is defined by antigens on the red cell and the antibodies already in plasma.

| Type | RBC antigen | Plasma antibodies | Can receive from |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | A | anti-B | A, O |
| B | B | anti-A | B, O |
| AB | A and B | none | all — universal recipient |
| O | none | anti-A and anti-B | O only — universal donor |

**Rh** is a separate antigen, usually D. Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure. That matters in pregnancy: an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus can be sensitized at delivery and attack a later Rh-positive fetus — **hemolytic disease of the newborn**, prevented by giving **RhoGAM (anti-D immune globulin)** at about `28` weeks and after delivery.

> **Key:** Transfusion reaction happens when the recipient's antibodies meet donor antigen. That is why the recipient's plasma, not the donor's, sets the rules.
keyPoints: Hematocrit is about 42–52% in men, 37–47% in women; plasma is about 55% of blood volume.
Albumin supplies colloid osmotic pressure; losing it causes edema.
EPO from the kidney rises when tissue oxygen falls, driving red cell production.
Coagulation converts prothrombin to thrombin, then fibrinogen to fibrin.
Type O is the universal red-cell donor; type AB is the universal recipient.

checks.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease is anemic despite adequate iron. The most likely cause is:
checks.why: The kidney makes EPO, so kidney failure removes the signal for erythropoiesis. Bilirubin is a breakdown product, and platelets and vitamin K affect clotting, not red cell production.

checks.q: A type B patient is transfused with type A blood. What happens?
choices: Nothing, because B is a universal recipient
The recipient's anti-A antibodies agglutinate the donor cells
The donor's anti-B antibodies destroy the recipient's marrow
checks.why: A type B person already carries anti-A antibodies, which attack the transfused A antigen immediately. AB is the universal recipient, not B, and the reaction is driven by recipient antibody.

checks.q: Which cell type is most abundant in a normal white blood cell differential and rises first in acute bacterial infection?
checks.why: Neutrophils make up 60–70% and are the first phagocytes to arrive. Lymphocytes are second in abundance and dominate viral responses; eosinophils rise with parasites and allergy.

lessons.title: The heart: anatomy, conduction, and the cardiac cycle
lessons.body:
## Anatomy

The heart sits in the mediastinum, about two-thirds left of midline, apex pointing down and left to the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. The **pericardium** is a fibrous sac with a serous parietal and visceral (epicardium) layer and `15–50 mL` of fluid between them. Wall layers: epicardium, **myocardium** (the thick muscle, thickest in the left ventricle), endocardium.

Four chambers: right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and coronary sinus; right ventricle pumps to the lungs; left atrium receives from four pulmonary veins; left ventricle pumps to the body.

Valves keep flow one-way. **Atrioventricular valves**: tricuspid on the right, **bicuspid (mitral)** on the left, anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles so they cannot invert. **Semilunar valves**: pulmonary and aortic, with no chordae.

> **Key:** Pathway to memorize cold — vena cava, right atrium, tricuspid, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta.

The myocardium feeds itself through the **coronary arteries**, the first branches off the aorta, filling during **diastole**. Left coronary gives the anterior interventricular (LAD) and circumflex branches; the right coronary gives the marginal and posterior interventricular branches.

## Cardiac muscle

Striated, one or two central nuclei, joined by **intercalated discs** carrying desmosomes (mechanical) and gap junctions (electrical), so the heart behaves as a **functional syncytium**. Cardiac cells have a long absolute refractory period of about `250 ms`, which makes tetanus impossible — a heart that could cramp could not pump.

## Conduction

**SA node** (right atrial wall, `60–100` per minute) to **AV node** (delays about `0.1 s` so atria empty first) to **bundle of His** to **right and left bundle branches** to **Purkinje fibers** in the ventricular walls. Intrinsic backup rates: AV node `40–60`, Purkinje `20–40`. Autorhythmic cells have unstable resting potentials — slow sodium leak produces the pacemaker potential, calcium influx causes depolarization, potassium efflux repolarizes.

## ECG basics

- **P wave**: atrial depolarization.
- **QRS complex**: ventricular depolarization; atrial repolarization is hidden inside it.
- **T wave**: ventricular repolarization.
- **PR interval** `0.12–0.20 s` is atrial depolarization plus the AV delay. **QRS** under `0.12 s`.

Rate is normally `60–100/min`; under `60` is bradycardia, over `100` tachycardia.

## The cardiac cycle

One cycle at `75/min` lasts about `0.8 s`. Atrial systole (`0.1 s`) tops off ventricles that are already about `70%` full from passive filling. Ventricular systole (`0.3 s`) begins with **isovolumetric contraction** — all valves shut, pressure rising, no volume change — then ejection when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about `80 mmHg`). Then **isovolumetric relaxation** and filling (`0.4 s`).

Heart sounds: **S1 (lubb)** is AV valves closing at the start of ventricular systole; **S2 (dupp)** is semilunar valves closing at its end. A **murmur** is turbulent flow, from a stenotic (narrowed) or incompetent (leaking) valve.

## Cardiac output

`CO = HR x SV`. Typical resting values: `70 beats/min x 70 mL = about 4,900 mL/min`, roughly `5 L/min` — the entire blood volume every minute. Stroke volume is end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume, about `120 - 50 = 70 mL`; **ejection fraction** is `SV/EDV`, normally `55–70%`.

Three things set stroke volume:

- **Preload**: how much the ventricle is stretched before contracting. The **Frank-Starling law** says more stretch means more forceful contraction, which is how the heart automatically matches output to venous return.
- **Contractility**: force at a given stretch. Sympathetic stimulation, epinephrine, and calcium increase it; acidosis and some drugs decrease it.
- **Afterload**: the pressure the ventricle must beat against. Hypertension raises it and lowers stroke volume.

Heart rate is set by the **cardiac centers in the medulla**: sympathetic fibers raise rate and contractility, the vagus lowers rate. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch feed them.

> **On the exam:** If cardiac output must rise and heart rate is fixed, the only remaining variable is stroke volume — and the fastest lever on stroke volume is preload.
keyPoints: SA node 60–100, AV node 40–60, Purkinje 20–40 beats per minute.
P wave is atrial depolarization, QRS ventricular depolarization, T wave ventricular repolarization.
Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume, about 5 L/min at rest.
Frank-Starling law: greater end-diastolic stretch produces a more forceful contraction.
S1 is AV valve closure, S2 is semilunar valve closure; coronary arteries fill during diastole.

checks.q: During isovolumetric contraction, which statement is true?
choices: The AV valves are open and blood is filling the ventricle
All four valves are closed and ventricular volume does not change
The semilunar valves are open and blood is ejected
checks.why: Pressure rises with every valve shut, so no volume moves. Ejection begins only once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic and pulmonary pressure.

checks.q: Heart rate is 80/min, end-diastolic volume 130 mL, end-systolic volume 60 mL. Cardiac output is:
checks.why: Stroke volume is 130 minus 60, which is 70 mL; 70 times 80 equals 5,600 mL or 5.6 L/min. Multiplying by EDV instead of stroke volume gives the 10.4 distractor.

checks.q: Damage to the AV node that blocks all conduction to the ventricles produces:
choices: Ventricles paced by Purkinje fibers at about 20–40 per minute
Atria that stop while ventricles speed up
A normal rate with a shortened PR interval
checks.why: Lower pacemakers take over at their slower intrinsic rates when the signal from above is blocked. The atria continue at the SA node rate, so the two chambers beat independently.

lessons.title: Blood vessels, hemodynamics, and blood pressure regulation
lessons.body:
## Vessel structure

Three tunics in arteries and veins: **tunica intima** (endothelium, smooth so blood does not clot), **tunica media** (smooth muscle and elastin — the layer that constricts and dilates, thickest in arteries), **tunica externa** (collagen anchoring).

- **Elastic (conducting) arteries**: aorta and its big branches. They stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, which is what keeps blood moving between beats.
- **Muscular (distributing) arteries**: deliver to organs.
- **Arterioles**: the **resistance vessels**. Small radius changes here dominate blood pressure.
- **Capillaries**: one cell thick, the only site of exchange. Continuous (most), fenestrated (kidney, intestine, endocrine glands), sinusoidal (liver, spleen, marrow).
- **Venules and veins**: thin walls, wide lumens, **valves**. Veins hold about `65%` of blood volume, so they are the **capacitance vessels**.

Veins move blood against gravity with the **skeletal muscle pump**, the **respiratory pump**, and valves. Failed valves give varicose veins.

## Flow, pressure, resistance

`F = ΔP / R`. Flow rises with the pressure difference and falls with resistance. Resistance depends on blood viscosity, vessel length, and above all **radius to the fourth power** — halve a radius and resistance rises `16` times.

Pressure falls steadily around the circuit: aorta about `120/80 mmHg`, arterioles a steep drop, capillaries about `35` falling to `17 mmHg`, vena cava near `0`. **Pulse pressure** is systolic minus diastolic, about `40 mmHg`. **Mean arterial pressure (MAP)** is approximately `diastolic + 1/3 of pulse pressure`, so `80 + 13 = about 93 mmHg`. MAP must stay above roughly `60 mmHg` to perfuse organs.

> **Key:** `MAP = CO x TPR`. Every blood pressure mechanism in the course works on one of those two terms.

## Capillary exchange

Three mechanisms: diffusion (the main one), transcytosis, and bulk flow.

Bulk flow is a tug-of-war. **Hydrostatic pressure** pushes fluid out of the capillary, high at the arterial end (about `35 mmHg`) and lower at the venous end (about `17 mmHg`). **Colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure** from plasma albumin pulls fluid back in at a steady `25 mmHg`. So fluid leaves at the arterial end and returns at the venous end, with roughly `3 L/day` left behind and carried home by lymphatics.

**Edema** follows from any imbalance: raised hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous obstruction), lowered oncotic pressure (liver failure or malnutrition reducing albumin, kidney loss of protein), leaky capillaries (inflammation), or blocked lymphatics.

## Named vessels

**Arteries**: aorta gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian. Carotids divide into internal (brain) and external (face). Subclavian becomes axillary, then brachial (where you take a blood pressure), then radial and ulnar. Descending aorta gives celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, renal, gonadal, inferior mesenteric, then splits into common iliacs, which become internal and external iliac, then femoral, popliteal, and the tibial arteries. Cerebral circulation is joined by the **circle of Willis**, a redundant ring fed by internal carotids and vertebral arteries.

**Veins**: superior vena cava drains head, neck, arms and upper thorax (internal jugular, subclavian, brachiocephalic, azygos). Inferior vena cava drains everything below (hepatic, renal, gonadal, common iliac). The **hepatic portal system** is the exception to the rule: veins from the intestines, spleen and pancreas drain into the liver first, so nutrients and toxins are processed before reaching the systemic circulation.

## Regulating blood pressure

**Short term, seconds — neural.** Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire faster when pressure rises; the medulla responds with reduced sympathetic output and increased vagal tone, so heart rate, contractility, and vasoconstriction all fall. Drop the pressure and the reflex reverses. Chemoreceptors respond to low oxygen or high `CO2` with vasoconstriction.

**Long term, hours to days — hormonal and renal.** The **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)**: low renal perfusion releases renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which ACE (mostly in the lung) converts to **angiotensin II** — a powerful vasoconstrictor that also triggers aldosterone (sodium and water retention), ADH, and thirst. **ADH** conserves water. **Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)** from stretched atria does the opposite: excrete sodium and water, vasodilate, lower pressure.

> **Trap:** The baroreceptor reflex resets within days at a new pressure, which is why it cannot correct chronic hypertension.
keyPoints: Resistance varies with the fourth power of radius; arterioles are the main resistance vessels.
MAP is roughly diastolic plus one third of pulse pressure, and MAP equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance.
Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out; albumin's 25 mmHg oncotic pressure pulls it back in.
Veins hold about 65% of blood volume and depend on valves and the skeletal muscle pump.
RAAS raises pressure through vasoconstriction and sodium retention; ANP lowers it.

checks.q: Blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg. What is the approximate mean arterial pressure?
checks.why: Pulse pressure is 60; one third of that is 20; 70 plus 20 equals 90. Averaging systolic and diastolic gives the wrong answer because diastole lasts longer than systole.

checks.q: A patient with liver failure has low plasma albumin and develops generalized edema. The mechanism is:
checks.why: Albumin generates the inward pull that returns fluid to the capillary; losing it leaves fluid in the interstitium. Hydrostatic causes come from heart failure or venous obstruction instead.

checks.q: A person stands up quickly and blood pressure briefly falls. The baroreceptor reflex responds by:
choices: Increasing vagal tone and slowing the heart
Decreasing sympathetic output to the vessels
Increasing sympathetic output, raising heart rate and vasoconstriction
checks.why: Falling pressure means fewer baroreceptor impulses, which releases the brake on sympathetic outflow. Increased vagal tone and ANP release are responses to high pressure, not low.

lessons.title: Lymphatic system and immunity
lessons.body:
## The lymphatic system

Three jobs: return the roughly `3 L/day` of fluid that capillaries leave behind, absorb dietary fat, and house immune cells.

Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended tubes with overlapping endothelial flaps that act as one-way valves. **Lacteals** in the intestinal villi absorb fat as chyle. Fluid flows capillaries to collecting vessels to trunks to two ducts: the **right lymphatic duct** drains the right arm and right head and thorax; the **thoracic duct** drains everything else. Both empty into the subclavian veins. There is no pump — flow depends on skeletal muscle, breathing, and valves.

Lymphoid organs: **lymph nodes** filter lymph (cortex holds B cell follicles, medulla holds plasma cells); the **spleen** filters blood and recycles red cells; the **thymus** matures T cells and shrinks after puberty; **tonsils**, **Peyer patches** and the appendix guard mucosal surfaces.

## Innate immunity — fast and nonspecific

**First line**: skin, mucous membranes, acid, lysozyme, normal flora.

**Second line**:

- **Phagocytes** — neutrophils first, then macrophages.
- **Natural killer (NK) cells** kill virus-infected and tumor cells that stop displaying self markers.
- **Inflammation**: redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function, all from histamine-driven vasodilation and increased permeability. It delivers cells and clotting proteins and walls off spread.
- **Fever**: pyrogens raise the hypothalamic set point; higher temperature slows microbial growth and speeds repair.
- **Complement**: about `20` plasma proteins that, once triggered, lyse cells via the membrane attack complex, opsonize for phagocytosis, and amplify inflammation.
- **Interferons**: virus-infected cells warn neighbors to make antiviral proteins.

## Adaptive immunity — slow, specific, and remembered

Two arms. **Humoral (antibody-mediated)** immunity uses B cells against extracellular pathogens. **Cellular (cell-mediated)** immunity uses T cells against infected cells, cancer, and transplants.

**Antigens** are what the system recognizes; the specific piece a receptor binds is the **epitope**. A small molecule that is only immunogenic once it binds a larger carrier protein is a **hapten**, which is how poison ivy and some drug allergies work.

**B cells** mature in bone marrow. On activation they proliferate into **plasma cells** that secrete antibody and **memory B cells**.

**T cells** mature in the thymus. **Helper T (CD4)** cells are the coordinators — they recognize antigen presented on MHC II by dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, and release cytokines that activate almost everything else. **Cytotoxic T (CD8)** cells recognize antigen on MHC I, present on every nucleated cell, and kill the infected cell with perforin and granzymes. **Regulatory T cells** shut the response down. HIV destroys CD4 cells, which is why one lost cell type collapses the whole response.

## Antibodies

Y-shaped immunoglobulins with two heavy and two light chains, variable regions at the tips that bind antigen and a constant region that determines class.

| Class | Where and what |
|---|---|
| IgG | `75–85%` of serum antibody; the memory antibody; the only one crossing the placenta |
| IgM | First made in a primary response; a pentamer; best complement activator |
| IgA | Secretions — saliva, tears, mucus, breast milk |
| IgE | Bound to mast cells and basophils; allergy and parasites |
| IgD | B cell surface receptor |

Antibodies do not kill directly. They **neutralize**, **agglutinate**, **precipitate**, and **activate complement** — often abbreviated as fixing, and all four make the pathogen easier to remove.

## Primary versus secondary response

The primary response takes `3–6` days to produce mostly IgM at a low peak. A second exposure produces a response in hours, dominated by IgG, at a much higher and longer-lasting titer. That difference is the entire basis of **vaccination**.

**Active immunity** means you made the antibodies — natural (infection) or artificial (vaccine), and it includes memory. **Passive immunity** means you received them — natural (placental IgG, breast milk IgA) or artificial (immune globulin, antivenom), it works immediately and lasts weeks to months with no memory.

> **Trap:** Passive immunity is fast but temporary, and it never protects you the second time. Active immunity is slow but has memory.

## Hypersensitivity

- **Type I, immediate**: IgE on mast cells, histamine release. Hay fever, hives, anaphylaxis within minutes.
- **Type II, cytotoxic**: IgG or IgM against cell surface antigen. Transfusion reaction, hemolytic disease of the newborn.
- **Type III, immune complex**: antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissue. Lupus, some glomerulonephritis.
- **Type IV, delayed**: T cell mediated, `12–72` hours. TB skin test, poison ivy, contact dermatitis.
keyPoints: Lymphatics return about 3 L/day of filtered fluid; the thoracic duct drains all but the right upper body.
Innate immunity is fast and nonspecific: phagocytes, NK cells, inflammation, fever, complement, interferon.
Helper T (CD4) cells read MHC II and coordinate; cytotoxic T (CD8) cells read MHC I and kill.
IgM is first, IgG is most abundant and crosses the placenta, IgA is in secretions, IgE causes allergy.
Active immunity has memory and is slow; passive immunity is immediate and temporary.

checks.q: A person is bitten by a venomous snake and receives antivenom. This is an example of:
checks.why: Preformed antibodies given by injection act immediately but leave no memory, which is artificial passive immunity. A vaccine would be artificial active immunity.

checks.q: HIV selectively destroys CD4 cells. Why is that so devastating?
choices: CD4 cells directly kill all pathogens
Helper T cells coordinate both B cell and cytotoxic T cell responses
CD4 cells make all the body's antibodies
CD4 cells form the membrane attack complex
checks.why: Helper T cells release the cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so losing them disables both arms of adaptive immunity. Plasma cells make antibody and complement forms the attack complex.

checks.q: A tuberculin skin test read at 48 hours shows firm induration. This is which hypersensitivity type?
checks.why: The delay of 12 to 72 hours and the T cell mechanism define type IV. Type I reactions appear within minutes and are IgE-driven.

lessons.title: Respiratory system: mechanics, volumes, gas exchange, and control
lessons.body:
## Anatomy

The **conducting zone** moves and conditions air: nose, pharynx (naso-, oro-, laryngo-), larynx (thyroid cartilage, cricoid, epiglottis, vocal folds), trachea (`16–20` C-shaped cartilage rings, open side posterior so the esophagus can expand), bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles. It warms, humidifies and filters air but does no gas exchange — that volume is **anatomic dead space**, about `150 mL`.

The **respiratory zone** does exchange: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, about `300 million` **alveoli** with a combined surface of roughly `70 m2`. The **respiratory membrane** is only about `0.5 micrometers` thick: type I alveolar cell (simple squamous), fused basement membranes, capillary endothelium. **Type II cells** secrete **surfactant**, which lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse — its absence in premature infants causes respiratory distress syndrome.

The right lung has three lobes, the left has two plus the cardiac notch. The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, so aspirated objects go right.

## Mechanics

Breathing is **Boyle's law**: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related. Increase thoracic volume, intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric, air flows in.

**Quiet inspiration** is active: the diaphragm flattens (about `75%` of the work) and external intercostals lift the ribs. **Quiet expiration** is passive elastic recoil. Forced breathing recruits scalenes, sternocleidomastoid and pectoralis minor for inspiration, and abdominals and internal intercostals for expiration.

**Intrapleural pressure** is always about `4 mmHg` below intrapulmonary pressure — negative pressure created by the lung pulling in and the chest wall pulling out, held together by pleural fluid. Puncture the pleural space and that vacuum is lost: air enters and the lung collapses, a **pneumothorax**.

Airflow depends on **compliance** (how easily lungs expand; reduced in fibrosis), **airway resistance** (raised in asthma by bronchoconstriction), and **surface tension** (managed by surfactant).

## Volumes and capacities

| Measure | Typical adult |
|---|---|
| Tidal volume (TV) | `500 mL` |
| Inspiratory reserve (IRV) | `3,100 mL` |
| Expiratory reserve (ERV) | `1,200 mL` |
| Residual volume (RV) | `1,200 mL` |
| Vital capacity (TV+IRV+ERV) | `4,800 mL` |
| Total lung capacity | `6,000 mL` |

Residual volume cannot be exhaled and therefore cannot be measured by spirometry. **Minute ventilation** is `TV x rate` — `500 x 12 = 6,000 mL/min`. **Alveolar ventilation** subtracts dead space first: `(500 - 150) x 12 = 4,200 mL/min`, which is the number that matters. Slow deep breathing ventilates better than fast shallow breathing at the same minute volume.

> **Key:** Obstructive disease (asthma, COPD) means air cannot get out — `FEV1/FVC` falls. Restrictive disease (fibrosis) means lungs cannot expand — volumes fall but the ratio is preserved.

## Gas exchange

Gases move by partial pressure gradient (Dalton's law). Approximate values: alveolar `PO2 104 mmHg`, `PCO2 40`; venous blood arriving `PO2 40`, `PCO2 45`; blood leaving the lung `PO2 100`, `PCO2 40`. At the tissues the gradients reverse.

`CO2` diffuses about `20` times more readily than `O2` despite a smaller gradient because it is far more soluble.

## Transport

**Oxygen**: about `98.5%` bound to hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, `1.5%` dissolved. The **oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve** is S-shaped — flat on top, so `PO2` can fall from `100` to `60 mmHg` with saturation still near `90%`, and steep below that, so oxygen unloads readily at tissue pressures. The curve shifts **right** (unload more) with high `CO2`, low pH, high temperature, and high 2,3-BPG — the **Bohr effect**, which delivers extra oxygen exactly to working muscle.

**Carbon dioxide** travels three ways: about `70%` as **bicarbonate** (formed in the red cell by carbonic anhydrase, then exchanged out for chloride — the chloride shift), about `23%` bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, and `7%` dissolved.

## Control of breathing

Rhythm comes from the medulla's ventral respiratory group, with the pons smoothing transitions. The **central chemoreceptors** in the medulla monitor CSF pH, which tracks `PCO2` — and `CO2` is the normal minute-to-minute driver of ventilation, not oxygen. **Peripheral chemoreceptors** in the carotid and aortic bodies respond to oxygen only when `PaO2` falls below about `60 mmHg`.

> **Trap:** Hyperventilating blows off `CO2`, raising pH and causing the tingling and dizziness of respiratory alkalosis. The urge to breathe is a carbon dioxide urge.
keyPoints: Intrapleural pressure stays about 4 mmHg below intrapulmonary pressure; losing it collapses the lung.
Tidal volume 500 mL, dead space 150 mL, so alveolar ventilation is (500-150) times rate.
Surfactant from type II alveolar cells lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse.
About 98.5% of oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin; about 70% of CO2 travels as bicarbonate.
Central chemoreceptors sensing CO2 and CSF pH are the normal drive to breathe.

checks.q: A stab wound opens the pleural space. Why does the lung collapse?
choices: Negative intrapleural pressure is lost and elastic recoil pulls the lung inward
checks.why: The lung is held expanded only by the pressure gradient across the pleural space. Equalize it with atmosphere and the lung's own recoil collapses it.

checks.q: A patient breathes 300 mL tidal volume at 20 breaths per minute. With 150 mL dead space, alveolar ventilation is:
checks.why: Subtract dead space first: 300 minus 150 equals 150 mL, times 20 equals 3,000 mL/min. The 6,000 figure is minute ventilation and overstates useful ventilation badly.

checks.q: During heavy exercise, muscle tissue is warm, acidic and CO2-rich. The oxygen-hemoglobin curve shifts:
choices: Left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly
Right, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen to tissue
checks.why: Heat, acidity and CO2 all reduce hemoglobin's affinity, unloading more oxygen where it is needed — the Bohr effect. A left shift would trap oxygen in the blood.

lessons.title: Digestive system: motility, secretion, digestion and absorption
lessons.body:
## The plan

Six processes: ingestion, propulsion, mechanical breakdown, chemical digestion, absorption, defecation. The **alimentary canal** runs mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus. **Accessory organs** — teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas — contribute but food never passes through them.

## Wall histology

Four layers everywhere, inside out: **mucosa** (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), **submucosa** (vessels, glands, submucosal plexus), **muscularis externa** (inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle, with the myenteric plexus between them), **serosa** (visceral peritoneum). Those two nerve plexuses make up the **enteric nervous system**, which can run digestion on its own.

Two motility patterns: **peristalsis** propels; **segmentation** mixes.

## Mouth to stomach

Saliva is `1–1.5 L/day` with **salivary amylase** (starch) and lingual lipase. Chewing forms a bolus; swallowing has a voluntary buccal phase and an involuntary pharyngeal-esophageal phase in which the epiglottis closes the airway.

The **stomach** stores, kills microbes, and starts protein digestion. Regions: cardia, fundus, body, pylorus. It has a third oblique muscle layer for churning, and **rugae** that flatten as it fills to about `1.5 L`. Gastric glands hold:

- **Parietal cells**: `HCl` (pH `1.5–3.5`) and **intrinsic factor**, which is required to absorb vitamin `B12` in the ileum.
- **Chief cells**: **pepsinogen**, activated by acid to **pepsin** for protein.
- **Mucous neck cells**: alkaline mucus that keeps the stomach from digesting itself.
- **G cells**: **gastrin**, which drives acid secretion.

Gastric phases: **cephalic** (sight and smell, vagal), **gastric** (stretch and peptides, gastrin — the biggest contributor), **intestinal** (briefly stimulating, then inhibitory as chyme enters the duodenum).

## Small intestine — where absorption happens

`6 m` long: duodenum (`25 cm`), jejunum, ileum. Surface area is multiplied about `600`-fold by **circular folds (plicae)**, **villi**, and **microvilli (brush border)**. Villi contain a capillary bed and a **lacteal**.

Duodenal hormones run the accessory organs. **Secretin** responds to acid and calls for bicarbonate from the pancreas. **Cholecystokinin (CCK)** responds to fat and protein and calls for pancreatic enzymes plus gallbladder contraction, and relaxes the hepatopancreatic sphincter.

## Liver, gallbladder, pancreas

The **liver** has four lobes and is built of hexagonal **lobules** of hepatocyte plates around a central vein, with portal triads at the corners (hepatic artery branch, portal vein branch, bile duct). It receives blood twice — oxygenated from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich from the **hepatic portal vein**. Jobs: bile production, glucose buffering, plasma protein synthesis, detoxification, vitamin and iron storage, Kupffer cell phagocytosis.

**Bile** contains bile salts, bilirubin, cholesterol and phospholipids; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it. Bile salts do not digest fat — they **emulsify** it into droplets so lipase has surface area to work on.

The **pancreas** is the enzyme organ: amylase, lipase, nucleases, and proteases secreted as inactive zymogens (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase) activated only in the duodenum by enterokinase. It also sends `HCO3-` to neutralize acid so those enzymes can work near `pH 8`.

> **Trap:** The pancreas makes its proteases inactive on purpose. Activate them early and the organ digests itself — pancreatitis.

## Digestion and absorption by macromolecule

| Nutrient | Enzymes | Absorbed as | Route |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrate | Salivary and pancreatic amylase, then brush border maltase, sucrase, lactase | Monosaccharides | Capillary to portal vein |
| Protein | Pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, brush border peptidases | Amino acids, di- and tripeptides | Capillary to portal vein |
| Fat | Bile salt emulsification, then pancreatic lipase | Monoglycerides and fatty acids in micelles, reassembled into **chylomicrons** | Lacteal to lymph |
| Nucleic acid | Nucleases, then nucleosidases | Nucleotides | Capillary |

Water — about `9 L/day` counting secretions — is absorbed mostly in the small intestine by osmosis.

## Large intestine

Cecum, appendix, ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal. **Teniae coli**, **haustra** and epiploic appendages identify it on a model. It absorbs remaining water and electrolytes, hosts bacteria that make vitamin `K` and some B vitamins, and forms feces. **Mass movements** a few times a day push contents toward the rectum; defecation is a spinal reflex with voluntary control of the external anal sphincter.

> **On the exam:** Fat is the one macronutrient that does not go straight to the liver. It enters lymph as chylomicrons and reaches blood at the subclavian vein.
keyPoints: Four wall layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa; the enteric plexuses sit in submucosa and muscularis.
Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor; chief cells make pepsinogen; G cells make gastrin.
Secretin calls for pancreatic bicarbonate; CCK calls for enzymes and gallbladder contraction.
Bile emulsifies fat, it does not digest it; pancreatic lipase does the digesting.
Carbohydrate and protein absorb into portal blood; fat absorbs into lacteals as chylomicrons.

checks.q: A patient has had the stomach removed and later develops B12 deficiency anemia. The reason is loss of:
checks.why: Intrinsic factor is required for B12 absorption in the ileum, and only parietal cells make it. Pepsinogen and gastrin affect protein digestion and acid, not B12 uptake.

checks.q: Acidic chyme enters the duodenum. Which hormone is released and what does it do?
checks.why: Secretin responds to acid by calling for bicarbonate that neutralizes the duodenum. CCK responds to fat and protein instead, and gastrin would worsen the acid load.

checks.q: After a fatty meal, absorbed lipid reaches the bloodstream by which route?
choices: Villus capillary to the hepatic portal vein
Lacteal to lymph to the subclavian vein
Gastric veins to the inferior vena cava
checks.why: Chylomicrons are too large for capillaries, so they enter lacteals and travel by lymph. Carbohydrate and amino acids take the portal route to the liver.

lessons.title: Metabolism, nutrition, and thermoregulation
lessons.body:
Metabolism is every chemical reaction in the body. **Catabolism** breaks molecules down and releases energy; **anabolism** builds and consumes it. ATP is the currency between them.

## Glucose catabolism

Four stages.

1. **Glycolysis**, in the cytosol, no oxygen required: one glucose becomes two pyruvate, net `2` ATP and `2` NADH.
2. **Pyruvate oxidation**, in the mitochondrial matrix: pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA, releasing `CO2` and making NADH.
3. **Citric acid (Krebs) cycle**, in the matrix: acetyl CoA is dismantled to `CO2`, generating NADH, `FADH2`, and `2` ATP per glucose.
4. **Electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation**, on the inner mitochondrial membrane: NADH and `FADH2` drop electrons down the chain, pumped protons build a gradient, ATP synthase spins, and **oxygen is the final electron acceptor**, forming water.

Total is about `30–32` ATP per glucose aerobically. Without oxygen, the chain backs up, NADH cannot be recycled, and pyruvate is converted to **lactate** to keep glycolysis running at `2` ATP per glucose.

> **Key:** The only reason you must breathe is to give the electron transport chain a place to put its electrons. Stop that and ATP production collapses within minutes.

## Fat and protein

Fats are catabolized by **beta oxidation** into acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle — a huge yield, which is why fat stores energy so densely. When carbohydrate is unavailable for a long time, the liver converts excess acetyl CoA into **ketone bodies**, which the brain can use; uncontrolled that gives ketoacidosis.

Amino acids are **deaminated** first, producing ammonia that the liver converts to **urea** for the kidney to excrete. The carbon skeletons enter glycolysis or the Krebs cycle.

## Absorptive versus postabsorptive state

**Absorptive** (fed, insulin dominant): glucose is used and stored as glycogen, excess becomes fat, amino acids build protein. **Postabsorptive** (fasting, glucagon dominant): glycogenolysis first, then gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol, then fat mobilization — all to protect blood glucose because the brain normally uses only glucose.

## Liver's role in metabolism

The liver processes everything absorbed via the portal vein. It stores glycogen, makes glucose, makes plasma proteins and clotting factors, packages lipoproteins, detoxifies drugs and alcohol, and converts ammonia to urea. **LDL** carries cholesterol to tissues and deposits it in vessel walls; **HDL** carries it back to the liver.

## Nutrition basics

Energy yields: carbohydrate and protein `4 kcal/g`, fat `9 kcal/g`, alcohol `7 kcal/g`. Essential nutrients are those the body cannot make: `9` essential amino acids, two essential fatty acids (linoleic and alpha-linolenic), vitamins, and minerals.

Fat-soluble vitamins `A`, `D`, `E`, `K` are stored and can reach toxic levels. Water-soluble vitamins (B complex and `C`) are excreted and need regular intake. Classic deficiencies: `C` gives scurvy, `D` gives rickets and osteomalacia, `B12` gives pernicious anemia, iron gives microcytic anemia, iodine gives goiter.

## Metabolic rate

**Basal metabolic rate (BMR)** is energy use at rest, fasting, and at a comfortable temperature — roughly `1,600–1,800 kcal/day` in an average adult. It rises with thyroid hormone, muscle mass, fever (about `7%` per degree Fahrenheit), and sympathetic activity, and falls with age and starvation. **Total metabolic rate** adds activity and digestion.

## Thermoregulation

Core temperature runs about `37 C` (`98.6 F`) with a normal daily swing near `1 C`. The **hypothalamus** is the thermostat, reading core temperature directly and skin temperature through peripheral receptors.

Heat is lost by **radiation** (the largest share at rest), **conduction**, **convection**, and **evaporation** (the only route that works when ambient temperature exceeds body temperature).

Too hot: cutaneous vasodilation and sweating. Too cold: vasoconstriction, shivering (which can raise heat production several-fold), and in infants **nonshivering thermogenesis** in brown fat.

**Fever** is different from hyperthermia. Fever is the hypothalamic set point deliberately raised by pyrogens, so you shiver on the way up and sweat when it breaks. **Heat stroke** is set point intact but heat loss overwhelmed — core over `40 C`, altered mental status, often with sweating already failed.

> **Trap:** Shivering while febrile is not "being cold." The set point moved and the body is defending the new, higher target.
keyPoints: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP in the cytosol; total aerobic yield is about 30–32 ATP per glucose.
Oxygen's only job in metabolism is to be the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain.
Beta oxidation feeds fat into the Krebs cycle as acetyl CoA; excess acetyl CoA becomes ketone bodies.
The liver converts ammonia from deamination into urea for renal excretion.
Evaporation is the only heat-loss route that works when the environment is hotter than the body.

checks.q: Cyanide blocks the final enzyme of the electron transport chain. The immediate metabolic consequence is:
choices: Oxidative phosphorylation stops and cells shift to lactate production
Ketone bodies can no longer be made
The Krebs cycle speeds up to compensate
checks.why: Blocking the chain stops ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation and backs up NADH, forcing anaerobic glycolysis with lactate. The Krebs cycle also stalls because it cannot regenerate NAD+.

checks.q: A person has fasted for 18 hours. Which process is most responsible for maintaining blood glucose now?
choices: Glycogenolysis and then gluconeogenesis in the liver
checks.why: Glucagon mobilizes liver glycogen first and then makes new glucose from amino acids and glycerol. Insulin-driven storage and GLUT4 insertion both happen in the fed state.

checks.q: On a 40 C day with high humidity, the body's ability to lose heat is limited because:
choices: Evaporation of sweat is impaired by humidity, and it is the only route left
checks.why: When ambient temperature exceeds body temperature, radiation and conduction add heat rather than remove it, leaving evaporation — which humidity blocks. That combination is what makes heat stroke likely.

lessons.title: Urinary system, fluid balance, and acid-base
lessons.body:
## Anatomy

Two kidneys (retroperitoneal, the left slightly higher), two ureters, bladder, urethra. Cut a kidney and you see **cortex**, **medulla** with renal pyramids, papillae emptying into **minor and major calyces**, then the **renal pelvis** and ureter.

## The nephron

About `1 million` per kidney. Each has a **renal corpuscle** — a **glomerulus** of capillaries inside **Bowman (glomerular) capsule** — and a tubule: **proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)**, **loop of Henle** with descending and ascending limbs, **distal convoluted tubule (DCT)**, **collecting duct**. Cortical nephrons make up about `85%`; **juxtamedullary** nephrons have long loops and are what allow concentrated urine.

Blood path: renal artery to segmental to interlobar to arcuate to cortical radiate to **afferent arteriole** to glomerulus to **efferent arteriole** to **peritubular capillaries** or **vasa recta**, then out the renal vein. Two capillary beds in series is the structural trick that makes filtration then reabsorption possible.

## Three processes

**Filtration** happens only at the corpuscle and is passive and nonselective by size: water, ions, glucose, amino acids and urea pass; cells and plasma proteins do not. Net filtration pressure is about `10 mmHg` — glomerular hydrostatic pressure `55` minus capsular pressure `15` minus blood colloid osmotic pressure `30`.

**Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** is about `125 mL/min`, or `180 L/day`. Over `99%` of that is reabsorbed, leaving `1–2 L` of urine. GFR is defended three ways: **myogenic** (afferent arteriole constricts when stretched), **tubuloglomerular feedback** (the macula densa of the juxtaglomerular complex senses `NaCl` and adjusts arteriolar tone), and extrinsic **sympathetic** and **RAAS** control during stress.

**Reabsorption** returns what you need. The PCT does the bulk: `100%` of glucose and amino acids (via sodium cotransport), about `65%` of sodium and water, most bicarbonate. Glucose transporters saturate at a plasma glucose of about `180 mg/dL` — the **renal threshold** — which is why glycosuria appears in uncontrolled diabetes.

**Secretion** moves things from blood into the tubule: `H+`, `K+`, ammonium, creatinine, many drugs. It is how the kidney fine-tunes pH and clears what filtration missed.

## Concentrating urine

The **countercurrent mechanism** builds a medullary gradient from about `300 mOsm` in the cortex to `1,200 mOsm` deep in the medulla. The descending limb is permeable to water but not salt; the thick ascending limb pumps out `NaCl` but is impermeable to water. Urea recycling adds to the gradient, and the vasa recta preserve it.

Then **ADH** decides the outcome. With ADH, aquaporins go into the collecting duct, water follows the gradient out, and urine is concentrated to as much as `1,200 mOsm`. Without ADH, the duct stays impermeable and dilute urine near `50 mOsm` pours out.

**Aldosterone** acts on the DCT and collecting duct: reabsorb sodium (water follows), secrete potassium. **ANP** opposes it.

> **Key:** ADH controls water alone. Aldosterone controls sodium, and water follows sodium. Confusing the two wrecks half of the renal exam.

## Micturition

The bladder holds `500–600 mL`; stretch receptors fire around `200 mL`. The reflex is parasympathetic (`S2–S4`) contracting the detrusor and relaxing the internal urethral sphincter; the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.

## Fluid compartments

Total body water is about `60%` of body weight in men and `50%` in women. Two thirds is **intracellular fluid**; one third is **extracellular** — and of that, about `80%` is interstitial and `20%` plasma. The main intracellular cation is **potassium**; the main extracellular cation is **sodium**. Sodium determines extracellular volume, which is why sodium balance and blood pressure are the same conversation.

Normal ranges worth memorizing: sodium `135–145 mEq/L`, potassium `3.5–5.0 mEq/L`, calcium `9.0–10.5 mg/dL`, chloride `98–107 mEq/L`.

## Acid-base

Defended pH is `7.35–7.45`. Three lines of defense at three speeds: **chemical buffers** (bicarbonate, phosphate, protein) act in seconds; the **respiratory system** adjusts `CO2` in `1–3` minutes; the **kidneys** excrete `H+` and regenerate bicarbonate over hours to days — and only the kidneys can remove fixed acid.

Four disorders: **respiratory acidosis** (retained `CO2` — COPD, oversedation), **respiratory alkalosis** (hyperventilation, anxiety, high altitude), **metabolic acidosis** (diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acid, diarrhea losing bicarbonate), **metabolic alkalosis** (vomiting acid, excess antacid).

Compensation is the other system pushing back. Metabolic acidosis is compensated by fast deep breathing (**Kussmaul respirations**) blowing off `CO2`. Respiratory acidosis is compensated by renal bicarbonate retention over days.

> **Trap:** Compensation moves the pH back toward normal but never past it. If pH is `7.30`, acidosis is still the primary problem no matter what the other value shows.
keyPoints: GFR is about 125 mL/min or 180 L/day; over 99% is reabsorbed.
The PCT reabsorbs 100% of glucose and amino acids; the renal threshold for glucose is about 180 mg/dL.
ADH controls water permeability of the collecting duct; aldosterone controls sodium and potassium.
Total body water is about 60% of body weight: two thirds intracellular, one third extracellular.
Buffers act in seconds, lungs in minutes, kidneys in hours to days; only kidneys remove fixed acid.

checks.q: A patient's urine contains glucose. The most likely explanation is:
choices: The glomerulus filters glucose only when it is abnormal
Plasma glucose exceeded the transport maximum of about 180 mg/dL
checks.why: Glucose is always filtered and normally fully reabsorbed in the PCT, so glycosuria means the carriers saturated. ADH and aldosterone govern water and sodium, not glucose.

checks.q: A patient with head trauma stops producing ADH. Expected findings are:
choices: Small volumes of very concentrated urine
Large volumes of very dilute urine and thirst
checks.why: Without ADH the collecting duct is water-impermeable, so filtrate leaves as dilute urine — diabetes insipidus. Concentrated low-volume urine would indicate excess ADH instead.

checks.q: Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28 with elevated PCO2. This is:
checks.why: Low pH with high CO2 means the lungs are the source of the acid load, as in hypoventilation. Metabolic acidosis would show a low bicarbonate with a low or normal CO2 from compensation.

lessons.title: Reproductive systems, pregnancy, and inheritance
lessons.body:
## Male anatomy

**Testes** sit in the scrotum, held about `3 C` below core temperature because sperm production fails at body temperature; the dartos and cremaster muscles adjust that. Inside are **seminiferous tubules** lined by spermatogenic cells and **sustentacular (Sertoli) cells** that nurse them and form the blood-testis barrier. Between tubules, **interstitial (Leydig) cells** make **testosterone**.

Duct path to memorize: seminiferous tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, **epididymis** (sperm mature and are stored, about `20` days), **ductus (vas) deferens**, ejaculatory duct, urethra.

Accessory glands: **seminal vesicles** (about `60%` of semen; fructose for energy, prostaglandins), **prostate** (about `30%`; alkaline, citrate), **bulbourethral glands** (pre-ejaculate that neutralizes urethral acid). Ejaculate is `2–5 mL` with `20–150 million` sperm per mL.

**Spermatogenesis** takes about `64–72` days and runs continuously from puberty. A spermatogonium yields `4` spermatids, each becoming a sperm with a head (nucleus plus **acrosome** of enzymes), midpiece (mitochondria), and tail. **FSH** acts on Sertoli cells to support it; **LH** acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone.

## Female anatomy

**Ovaries** held by ovarian, suspensory and broad ligaments; **uterine (fallopian) tubes** with fimbriae, where fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla; **uterus** (fundus, body, cervix) with walls of perimetrium, **myometrium**, and **endometrium** (functional layer shed monthly, basal layer regenerates it); vagina; external genitalia (mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoris).

**Oogenesis** differs from spermatogenesis in three ways worth memorizing: it starts before birth and arrests, it produces only **one** viable ovum plus polar bodies, and the supply is finite — about `1–2 million` primary oocytes at birth, `400,000` at puberty, roughly `400` ever ovulated. Meiosis I completes just before ovulation; meiosis II completes only if a sperm penetrates.

## The ovarian and uterine cycles

Average `28` days, counted from the first day of menstruation.

**Ovarian cycle**. Follicular phase, days `1–13`: FSH drives follicle growth and rising **estrogen**. When estrogen is high and sustained, feedback flips positive and triggers the **LH surge**. **Ovulation** near day `14`. Luteal phase, days `15–28`: the ruptured follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, making **progesterone** plus estrogen. No pregnancy means it degenerates by day `26`, hormones fall, and the cycle restarts.

**Uterine cycle**. Menstrual phase days `1–5`: the functional layer sheds because progesterone fell. Proliferative phase days `6–14`: estrogen rebuilds the endometrium. Secretory phase days `15–28`: progesterone makes it glandular and receptive.

> **Key:** Estrogen builds the lining. Progesterone maintains it. Menstruation happens because progesterone was withdrawn.

## Fertilization and early development

Sperm must **capacitate** in the female tract. One sperm's acrosomal enzymes breach the corona radiata and zona pellucida; fusion triggers the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy. The **zygote** cleaves into a **morula**, becomes a **blastocyst** with an inner cell mass and trophoblast, and **implants** about day `6–7`.

The trophoblast secretes **human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**, which keeps the corpus luteum alive so progesterone does not fall — this is what a pregnancy test detects. The **placenta** takes over hormone production by weeks `8–12` and handles all exchange; fetal and maternal blood never mix.

Germ layers from gastrulation: **ectoderm** (nervous system, epidermis), **mesoderm** (muscle, bone, blood, kidney, heart), **endoderm** (gut lining, liver, pancreas, respiratory lining). Embryo through week `8`, fetus after. Pregnancy is `40` weeks from the last menstrual period, three trimesters.

Fetal shunts bypass the nonfunctional lungs and liver: **ductus venosus**, **foramen ovale**, **ductus arteriosus**. All close after the first breaths.

**Labor** has three stages — dilation (longest), expulsion, placental — and runs on positive feedback: stretch drives oxytocin, oxytocin drives contraction, contraction drives more stretch. **Prolactin** makes milk; **oxytocin** ejects it.

## Inheritance basics

Humans have `46` chromosomes, `23` pairs — `22` autosomal pairs plus sex chromosomes. Gametes are haploid (`23`). **Genotype** is the allele pair, **phenotype** the trait shown; **homozygous** is two matching alleles, **heterozygous** two different.

A cross of two heterozygotes (`Aa x Aa`) gives a `3:1` phenotype ratio and `1:2:1` genotype ratio. A carrier cross for a recessive disease such as cystic fibrosis gives a `25%` chance of an affected child.

**X-linked recessive** traits — hemophilia, red-green color blindness, Duchenne muscular dystrophy — appear far more in males, who have only one X and therefore no second copy to mask the allele. Other patterns: **incomplete dominance** (blended phenotype), **codominance** (both shown, as in AB blood type), and **polygenic** traits like height and skin color.

> **Trap:** Sex is determined by the father's gamete, because the mother contributes only an X. The `SRY` gene on the Y drives testis formation.
keyPoints: Sertoli cells nurse sperm and form the blood-testis barrier; Leydig cells make testosterone.
Spermatogenesis yields four sperm continuously; oogenesis yields one ovum from a finite, prenatal supply.
The LH surge triggers ovulation near day 14; the corpus luteum then makes progesterone.
hCG from the trophoblast sustains the corpus luteum and is what a pregnancy test detects.
Ectoderm makes nervous system and skin, mesoderm makes muscle bone and blood, endoderm makes gut and glands.

checks.q: Menstruation begins because:
choices: The corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls
checks.why: The functional endometrium depends on progesterone support, so its withdrawal causes shedding. Rising estrogen rebuilds the lining in the proliferative phase instead.

checks.q: Two parents are both carriers of an autosomal recessive disease. The chance that any given child is affected is:
checks.why: A heterozygote cross gives one in four homozygous recessive offspring. The 50% figure describes carriers and 75% describes those showing the dominant phenotype.

checks.q: Which structure produces the hormone detected by a home pregnancy test, and what does that hormone do?
choices: Corpus luteum; produces hCG to maintain the placenta
Trophoblast of the blastocyst; produces hCG to maintain the corpus luteum
Anterior pituitary; produces LH to maintain the endometrium
Placenta; produces progesterone detected in urine
checks.why: The trophoblast secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum alive so progesterone continues and the lining is not shed. The corpus luteum is the target of hCG, not its source.

cards.front: How do water-soluble and lipid-soluble hormones differ in mechanism?
cards.back: Water-soluble hormones bind surface receptors and use second messengers like cyclic AMP — fast and short. Lipid-soluble hormones enter the cell, bind intracellular receptors, and alter gene transcription — slow and sustained.

cards.front: Which six hormones does the anterior pituitary produce?
cards.back: Growth hormone, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin. The posterior pituitary makes none — it stores and releases hypothalamic ADH and oxytocin.

cards.front: Trace the thyroid axis and its feedback.
cards.back: Hypothalamic TRH triggers pituitary TSH, which triggers thyroid T3 and T4. Rising T3 and T4 inhibit both TRH and TSH by negative feedback.

cards.front: What does aldosterone do, and where?
cards.back: In the distal tubule and collecting duct it reabsorbs sodium with water following and secretes potassium, raising blood volume and pressure.

cards.front: Contrast insulin and glucagon actions.
cards.back: Insulin lowers glucose through GLUT4 uptake, glycogenesis and lipogenesis. Glucagon raises it through hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

cards.front: How does diabetes insipidus differ from diabetes mellitus?
cards.back: Insipidus is an ADH problem causing large volumes of dilute urine with normal glucose. Mellitus is an insulin problem causing hyperglycemia and glycosuria.

cards.front: What is a normal hematocrit, and what is the buffy coat?
cards.back: About 42–52% in men and 37–47% in women. The buffy coat is the thin layer of white cells and platelets between plasma and packed red cells.

cards.front: Which plasma protein maintains colloid osmotic pressure, and what happens when it falls?
cards.back: Albumin. Low albumin reduces the inward pull at capillaries, so fluid stays in the interstitium and edema develops.

cards.front: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus or mitochondria?
cards.back: To maximize hemoglobin content and to avoid consuming the oxygen it transports. The tradeoff is a fixed lifespan of about 120 days.

cards.front: What stimulates erythropoietin release, and from where?
cards.back: Low tissue oxygen sensed by the kidney. EPO then drives red cell production in red bone marrow — the reason kidney failure causes anemia.

cards.front: List white blood cells from most to least abundant with their percentages.
cards.back: Neutrophils 60–70%, lymphocytes 20–25%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 2–4%, basophils under 1%.

cards.front: What are the three steps of hemostasis?
cards.back: Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, and coagulation converting prothrombin to thrombin then fibrinogen to fibrin.

cards.front: Which blood type is the universal donor and which the universal recipient, and why?
cards.back: Type O has no A or B antigens so it is the universal red cell donor. Type AB has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies so it is the universal recipient.

cards.front: Why is RhoGAM given to an Rh-negative pregnant woman?
cards.back: To prevent her from making anti-D antibodies after exposure to Rh-positive fetal blood, which would attack a later Rh-positive fetus. Given about 28 weeks and after delivery.

cards.front: Give the full path of blood through the heart and lungs.
cards.back: Venae cavae, right atrium, tricuspid, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta.

cards.front: What do chordae tendineae and papillary muscles do?
cards.back: They anchor the atrioventricular valve cusps so ventricular pressure cannot push them backward into the atria. Semilunar valves need no such support.

cards.front: Give the conduction pathway and the intrinsic rate of each pacemaker.
cards.back: SA node 60–100, AV node 40–60 with a 0.1 s delay, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers 20–40 per minute.

cards.front: What does each ECG wave represent?
cards.back: P wave is atrial depolarization, QRS is ventricular depolarization (hiding atrial repolarization), T wave is ventricular repolarization.

cards.front: What causes S1 and S2 heart sounds?
cards.back: S1 is closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular systole. S2 is closure of the semilunar valves at its end.

cards.front: Write the cardiac output equation with typical resting values.
cards.back: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: about 70 beats per minute times 70 mL, roughly 5 L per minute.

cards.front: What is ejection fraction and its normal range?
cards.back: Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, normally 55–70%. With EDV 120 mL and ESV 50 mL, SV is 70 mL and EF is about 58%.

cards.front: State the Frank-Starling law and why it matters.
cards.back: The more the ventricle is stretched by venous return, the more forcefully it contracts. It automatically matches cardiac output to the blood coming back.

cards.front: Name the three tunics of a vessel and what each does.
cards.back: Tunica intima is smooth endothelium, tunica media is smooth muscle and elastin that constricts and dilates, tunica externa is collagen that anchors.

cards.front: Why are arterioles called the resistance vessels?
cards.back: Resistance varies with the fourth power of radius, so small changes in arteriolar diameter produce large changes in peripheral resistance and blood pressure.

cards.front: How do you calculate mean arterial pressure?
cards.back: Diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure. For 120/80: pulse pressure 40, one third is about 13, MAP about 93 mmHg.

cards.front: What two forces govern capillary bulk flow?
cards.back: Hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, about 35 mmHg arterially and 17 mmHg venously. Colloid osmotic pressure from albumin pulls it back at about 25 mmHg.

cards.front: Name four mechanisms that produce edema.
cards.back: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, lowered plasma oncotic pressure, increased capillary permeability from inflammation, and blocked lymphatic drainage.

cards.front: What is the hepatic portal system and why does it exist?
cards.back: Veins from the intestines, spleen and pancreas drain into the liver before reaching the heart, so nutrients and toxins are processed before entering systemic circulation.

cards.front: Describe the baroreceptor reflex response to a fall in blood pressure.
cards.back: Fewer impulses from carotid sinus and aortic arch reach the medulla, so sympathetic output rises: heart rate, contractility and vasoconstriction all increase.

cards.front: Walk through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
cards.back: Low renal perfusion releases renin, which makes angiotensin I from angiotensinogen; ACE converts it to angiotensin II, which vasoconstricts and triggers aldosterone, ADH and thirst.

cards.front: What are the three functions of the lymphatic system?
cards.back: Return about 3 L/day of filtered fluid to the blood, absorb dietary fat through intestinal lacteals, and house immune cells and lymphoid organs.

cards.front: What does the thoracic duct drain, and what does the right lymphatic duct drain?
cards.back: The thoracic duct drains everything except the right arm and right side of head and thorax, which the right lymphatic duct handles. Both empty into subclavian veins.

cards.front: Name five components of the innate second line of defense.
cards.back: Phagocytes, natural killer cells, inflammation, fever, and antimicrobial proteins including complement and interferons.

cards.front: How do helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells differ?
cards.back: Helper (CD4) cells read antigen on MHC II and release cytokines that coordinate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Cytotoxic (CD8) cells read MHC I on any nucleated cell and kill it with perforin and granzymes.

cards.front: Match each antibody class to its role: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD.
cards.back: IgG is most abundant and crosses the placenta, IgM is first in a primary response, IgA is in secretions, IgE drives allergy on mast cells, IgD is a B cell surface receptor.

cards.front: How do antibodies actually defeat a pathogen?
cards.back: They neutralize, agglutinate, precipitate, and activate complement. They do not kill directly — they mark and immobilize so other systems can destroy.

cards.front: Compare the primary and secondary immune responses.
cards.back: Primary takes 3–6 days and is mostly IgM at a low peak. Secondary happens in hours, is dominated by IgG, and reaches a much higher, longer-lasting titer.

cards.front: Give one example each of natural active, artificial active, natural passive, and artificial passive immunity.
cards.back: Natural active is recovering from infection, artificial active is a vaccine, natural passive is placental IgG or breast milk IgA, artificial passive is immune globulin or antivenom.

cards.front: Name the four hypersensitivity types with an example of each.
cards.back: Type I immediate IgE (anaphylaxis), type II cytotoxic (transfusion reaction), type III immune complex (lupus), type IV delayed T cell (TB skin test, poison ivy).

cards.front: What is the respiratory membrane made of, and how thick is it?
cards.back: Type I alveolar cell, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium — about 0.5 micrometers thick, across roughly 70 square meters of alveolar surface.

cards.front: What does surfactant do and which cell makes it?
cards.back: Type II alveolar cells make it. It lowers alveolar surface tension so small alveoli do not collapse; absence in premature infants causes respiratory distress syndrome.

cards.front: Explain quiet inspiration using Boyle's law.
cards.back: The diaphragm flattens and external intercostals lift the ribs, increasing thoracic volume, which lowers intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric so air flows in.

cards.front: Why is intrapleural pressure negative, and what happens if it is lost?
cards.back: The lung's inward recoil and the chest wall's outward pull create about -4 mmHg relative to intrapulmonary pressure. Losing it lets the lung collapse — pneumothorax.

cards.front: How is alveolar ventilation calculated and why does it beat minute ventilation?
cards.back: Subtract dead space first: (tidal volume minus 150 mL) times rate. It reflects air that actually reaches alveoli, so slow deep breathing outperforms fast shallow breathing.

cards.front: How is oxygen carried in blood, and how is carbon dioxide carried?
cards.back: Oxygen: about 98.5% on hemoglobin, 1.5% dissolved. Carbon dioxide: about 70% as bicarbonate, 23% on hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, 7% dissolved.

cards.front: What shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right, and what does that accomplish?
cards.back: High CO2, low pH, high temperature and high 2,3-BPG. The Bohr effect unloads more oxygen exactly where metabolism is highest.

cards.front: What normally drives the urge to breathe?
cards.back: Rising carbon dioxide, sensed as falling CSF pH by central chemoreceptors in the medulla. Oxygen becomes a drive only when PaO2 drops below about 60 mmHg.

cards.front: Name the four layers of the alimentary canal wall from inside out.
cards.back: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa. The submucosal and myenteric nerve plexuses form the enteric nervous system.

cards.front: Match each gastric cell to its secretion: parietal, chief, mucous neck, G cell.
cards.back: Parietal makes HCl and intrinsic factor, chief makes pepsinogen, mucous neck cells make protective alkaline mucus, G cells make gastrin.

cards.front: What are the three phases of gastric secretion?
cards.back: Cephalic from sight and smell via the vagus, gastric from stretch and peptides via gastrin (the largest share), and intestinal which briefly stimulates then inhibits.

cards.front: Contrast the actions of secretin and cholecystokinin.
cards.back: Secretin responds to duodenal acid and calls for pancreatic bicarbonate. CCK responds to fat and protein, calling for pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction.

cards.front: What do bile salts actually do to fat?
cards.back: They emulsify it, breaking large globules into small droplets so pancreatic lipase has far more surface area to work on. They do not digest fat themselves.

cards.front: Why does the pancreas secrete proteases as inactive zymogens?
cards.back: So it does not digest itself. Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin by enterokinase in the duodenum, and trypsin then activates the rest.

cards.front: Which three structures multiply small intestine surface area, and by roughly how much?
cards.back: Circular folds (plicae circulares), villi, and microvilli of the brush border — together about a 600-fold increase.

cards.front: By what route does each macronutrient leave the intestine?
cards.back: Monosaccharides and amino acids enter villus capillaries and go to the liver by the hepatic portal vein. Fat becomes chylomicrons and enters lacteals, reaching blood at the subclavian vein.

cards.front: How much ATP does one glucose yield in glycolysis versus complete aerobic respiration?
cards.back: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Complete aerobic breakdown yields about 30 to 32 ATP per glucose.

cards.front: What is oxygen's role in cellular respiration?
cards.back: It is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain, forming water. Without it the chain backs up, NAD+ is not regenerated, and ATP production collapses.

cards.front: Where does each stage of glucose catabolism occur?
cards.back: Glycolysis in the cytosol; pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

cards.front: What happens to amino acids used for fuel?
cards.back: They are deaminated, producing ammonia that the liver converts to urea for renal excretion. The remaining carbon skeleton enters glycolysis or the Krebs cycle.

cards.front: Name the four routes of heat loss and the one that works in a hot environment.
cards.back: Radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation. Only evaporation removes heat when ambient temperature exceeds body temperature.

cards.front: How does fever differ from heat stroke?
cards.back: Fever is a deliberate hypothalamic set point increase driven by pyrogens, so shivering occurs on the way up. Heat stroke is a normal set point overwhelmed, with core above 40 C and altered mental status.

cards.front: List the nephron segments in order.
cards.back: Glomerulus in Bowman capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, descending and ascending loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct.

cards.front: What is normal GFR, and how much filtrate becomes urine?
cards.back: About 125 mL/min or 180 L/day. Over 99% is reabsorbed, leaving 1 to 2 L of urine per day.

cards.front: How is net filtration pressure calculated at the glomerulus?
cards.back: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure of about 55 mmHg minus capsular pressure 15 minus blood colloid osmotic pressure 30, giving about 10 mmHg outward.

cards.front: What does the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorb?
cards.back: All filtered glucose and amino acids by sodium cotransport, about 65% of sodium and water, and most bicarbonate. It is the bulk-reabsorption segment.

cards.front: How does the loop of Henle build the medullary gradient?
cards.back: The descending limb is permeable to water but not salt; the thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out but is water-impermeable. This countercurrent multiplication reaches about 1,200 mOsm deep in the medulla.

cards.front: Distinguish what ADH controls from what aldosterone controls.
cards.back: ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct and controls water alone. Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and secretes potassium in the distal tubule, and water follows sodium.

cards.front: How is total body water distributed?
cards.back: About 60% of body weight in men and 50% in women. Two thirds is intracellular; of the extracellular third, about 80% is interstitial and 20% is plasma.

cards.front: Give normal serum sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride values.
cards.back: Sodium 135–145 mEq/L, potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L, calcium 9.0–10.5 mg/dL, chloride 98–107 mEq/L.

cards.front: Name the three lines of acid-base defense and their speeds.
cards.back: Chemical buffers act in seconds, the respiratory system adjusts CO2 in one to three minutes, and the kidneys excrete acid and regenerate bicarbonate over hours to days.

cards.front: Identify the acid-base disorder: pH 7.30 with a low bicarbonate and rapid deep breathing.
cards.back: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation. Kussmaul respirations blow off CO2 to pull pH back toward normal, but pH stays below 7.35 because compensation never overcorrects.

cards.front: What do Sertoli and Leydig cells do?
cards.back: Sertoli (sustentacular) cells nourish developing sperm and form the blood-testis barrier under FSH. Leydig (interstitial) cells produce testosterone under LH.
