cards.front: How do spermatogenesis and oogenesis differ?
cards.back: Spermatogenesis is continuous from puberty and yields four sperm per cell. Oogenesis starts before birth from a finite supply, arrests, and yields one ovum plus polar bodies.

cards.front: What triggers ovulation, and what forms afterward?
cards.back: A surge of luteinizing hormone near day 14, driven by sustained high estrogen flipping feedback to positive. The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone.

cards.front: Match the uterine cycle phases to the hormone driving each.
cards.back: Menstrual days 1–5 from progesterone withdrawal, proliferative days 6–14 driven by estrogen, secretory days 15–28 driven by progesterone from the corpus luteum.

cards.front: Where does fertilization normally occur, and what blocks polyspermy?
cards.back: The ampulla of the uterine tube. Sperm fusion triggers the cortical reaction, which alters the zona pellucida so no other sperm can enter.

cards.front: What does hCG do, and what makes it?
cards.back: The trophoblast of the blastocyst makes it. It keeps the corpus luteum alive so progesterone continues and the endometrium is not shed — the target of a pregnancy test.

cards.front: Which structures come from each primary germ layer?
cards.back: Ectoderm gives nervous system and epidermis; mesoderm gives muscle, bone, blood, heart and kidney; endoderm gives gut lining, liver, pancreas and respiratory lining.

cards.front: Name the three fetal circulatory shunts and what each bypasses.
cards.back: Ductus venosus bypasses the liver, foramen ovale shunts right atrium to left atrium, ductus arteriosus connects pulmonary trunk to aorta. All bypass the nonfunctional lungs or liver.

cards.front: Why do X-linked recessive conditions appear far more often in males?
cards.back: Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed with no second copy to mask it. Examples include hemophilia and red-green color blindness.

quiz.q: A hormone produces its effect within seconds by activating enzymes already present in the cytoplasm. This hormone most likely:
choices: Is a steroid acting on DNA
Required a carrier protein in blood
Diffused through the membrane to a nuclear receptor
Bound a surface receptor and used a second messenger
quiz.why: Speed and reliance on existing enzymes point to cyclic AMP second-messenger signaling by a water-soluble hormone. Steroid action requires gene transcription and takes hours.

quiz.q: A patient has low cortisol and high ACTH. The lesion is in the:
quiz.why: A failing adrenal cortex cannot make cortisol, so feedback inhibition is lost and ACTH climbs. Pituitary failure would give low ACTH along with low cortisol.

quiz.q: An untreated type 1 diabetic has polyuria. The direct mechanism is:
choices: Glucose exceeding the renal threshold and holding water in the filtrate
quiz.why: Above about 180 mg/dL the tubular carriers saturate, so glucose stays in the filtrate and osmotically drags water with it. ADH is normal, and aldosterone retains sodium rather than losing it.

quiz.q: Blood is centrifuged. The layer between packed red cells and plasma contains:
quiz.why: The buffy coat holds leukocytes and platelets, which are less dense than erythrocytes. Albumin, globulins and fibrinogen are dissolved in the plasma layer above.

quiz.q: A person moves to high altitude. Two weeks later the hematocrit is higher. This is because:
choices: Bone marrow was damaged by hypoxia
Low tissue oxygen increased renal erythropoietin release
quiz.why: Hypoxia is the stimulus for EPO, which drives erythropoiesis — a negative feedback loop. Plasma volume actually falls initially, and affinity shifts do not change cell count.

quiz.q: In the coagulation cascade, thrombin's essential action is to:
quiz.why: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into the insoluble fibrin mesh that stabilizes the plug. Plasmin, not thrombin, dissolves clots later.

quiz.q: An Rh-negative woman delivers her first Rh-positive baby without complication, but her second Rh-positive pregnancy is affected. Why?
choices: The first baby sensitized her to produce anti-D antibodies
She was born with anti-D antibodies
Rh antigens appear only in later pregnancies
quiz.why: Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure, which typically occurs at the first delivery. Those IgG antibodies then cross the placenta in the next pregnancy.

quiz.q: Which valve prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium?
quiz.why: The mitral valve guards the left atrioventricular opening. The tricuspid does the same job on the right, and semilunar valves guard the arterial outflows.

quiz.q: The AV node delays the impulse by about 0.1 second. The functional reason is:
choices: To prevent tetanus of the ventricles
To slow the heart rate to 60 per minute
To let the atria finish contracting and fill the ventricles before ventricular systole
quiz.why: Without the delay, atria and ventricles would contract together and ventricular filling would be incomplete. Tetanus is prevented by the long refractory period instead.

quiz.q: A patient's ECG shows a normal P wave for every QRS, but the PR interval measures 0.26 seconds. This indicates:
choices: Delayed conduction through the AV node
quiz.why: The PR interval measures atrial depolarization plus AV nodal delay, and normal is 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. Since every P is followed by a QRS, ventricular depolarization is intact.

quiz.q: Severe tachycardia at 190 beats per minute reduces cardiac output. The reason is:
choices: Diastolic filling time shortens, reducing preload and stroke volume
quiz.why: Filling happens during diastole, and extreme rates cut that time so the ventricle enters systole underfilled. Reduced preload lowers stroke volume enough to offset the higher rate.

quiz.q: If an arteriole's radius is reduced by half, resistance to flow increases by approximately:
quiz.why: Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius, so halving the radius multiplies resistance by 2 to the fourth, or 16. This is why arterioles dominate blood pressure control.

quiz.q: Which vessels contain the largest share of the body's blood volume at rest?
quiz.why: Veins are thin-walled and distensible, holding about 65% of blood volume, which is why they are called capacitance vessels. Arteries hold a small fraction under high pressure.

quiz.q: A drug blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme. The expected effects include:
choices: Decreased angiotensin II, decreased aldosterone, and lower blood pressure
quiz.why: ACE makes angiotensin II, so blocking it removes both the vasoconstriction and the aldosterone signal, lowering pressure. Every listed distractor describes RAAS activation rather than inhibition.

quiz.q: At the venous end of a capillary, net fluid movement is inward because:
choices: Hydrostatic pressure has fallen below colloid osmotic pressure
Colloid osmotic pressure has risen sharply
quiz.why: Hydrostatic pressure drops from about 35 to 17 mmHg along the capillary while oncotic pressure stays near 25 mmHg, reversing the net direction. Oncotic pressure changes very little across the bed.

quiz.q: Nutrients absorbed from the small intestine reach the liver before the systemic circulation because of the:
quiz.why: The hepatic portal vein carries venous blood from gut, spleen and pancreas into the liver sinusoids for processing. The thoracic duct carries absorbed fat and bypasses the liver entirely.

quiz.q: A patient has had axillary lymph nodes removed and develops swelling of that arm. The mechanism is:
choices: Increased arterial pressure in the limb
Impaired lymphatic drainage of interstitial fluid
quiz.why: Lymphatics return the roughly 3 L/day capillaries leave behind, so removing the drainage route causes lymphedema. Albumin and arterial pressure are unchanged by node removal.

quiz.q: A virus-infected body cell displays viral peptide on MHC class I. Which cell destroys it?
quiz.why: CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize MHC I on any nucleated cell and kill it with perforin and granzymes. Helper T cells read MHC II and coordinate rather than kill.

quiz.q: A newborn is protected against measles for several months because of maternal antibodies crossing the placenta. This is:
quiz.why: IgG is the only class that crosses the placenta, and receiving antibodies rather than making them is passive immunity. IgA passes in breast milk, and IgE mediates allergy.

quiz.q: A person stung by a bee develops hives, wheezing, and hypotension within five minutes. This is:
quiz.why: Minutes-long onset with IgE-driven mast cell histamine release defines type I. Type IV reactions take 12 to 72 hours and cause induration rather than shock.

quiz.q: A patient breathes rapidly and shallowly at 500 mL of dead space-heavy breaths. Compared with slow deep breathing at the same minute ventilation, alveolar ventilation is:
choices: The same, because minute ventilation is equal
Lower, because dead space is subtracted from every breath
quiz.why: The 150 mL dead space is wasted on each breath, so more small breaths waste more total volume. Minute ventilation hides this, which is why alveolar ventilation is the meaningful number.

quiz.q: Which structure prevents alveolar collapse at the end of expiration?
choices: Surfactant from type II alveolar cells
quiz.why: Surfactant lowers surface tension so small alveoli do not empty into larger ones. Cartilage supports conducting airways and does not reach the alveoli.

quiz.q: During quiet inspiration, intrapulmonary pressure:
choices: Rises above atmospheric, pushing air out
Falls below atmospheric, drawing air in
quiz.why: Increasing thoracic volume lowers the pressure inside the lungs, and air flows down the gradient — Boyle's law. Pressure rises above atmospheric only during expiration.

quiz.q: Most carbon dioxide is transported in blood as:
choices: Bicarbonate ion formed by carbonic anhydrase in red cells
quiz.why: About 70% travels as bicarbonate after conversion inside the erythrocyte, then exits in exchange for chloride. Carbaminohemoglobin accounts for about 23% and dissolved gas only 7%.

quiz.q: An anxious patient hyperventilates and reports tingling around the mouth and fingers. The arterial blood gas would most likely show:
quiz.why: Blowing off CO2 removes acid and raises pH — respiratory alkalosis. Low pH with high CO2 describes hypoventilation, the opposite problem.

quiz.q: A patient after gastric bypass develops fat malabsorption with normal pancreatic enzyme levels. The most likely missing step is:
quiz.why: Without emulsification, lipase has too little surface area to act on even when present in normal amounts. Trypsin, lactase and glucose transport concern protein and carbohydrate, not fat.

quiz.q: Which hormone causes the gallbladder to contract and pancreatic enzymes to be released?
quiz.why: CCK responds to fat and protein in the duodenum. Secretin responds to acid and produces bicarbonate, while gastrin increases gastric acid secretion.

quiz.q: Pepsinogen is secreted rather than active pepsin because:
choices: The inactive form protects chief cells from self-digestion until acid activates it
The stomach lacks the enzyme to make pepsin
quiz.why: Secreting a zymogen keeps the protease inert inside the cell; gastric HCl converts it to pepsin in the lumen. The same logic protects the pancreas with trypsinogen.

quiz.q: A runner's muscles switch to lactate production during a sprint. The immediate reason is:
choices: Oxygen delivery cannot keep the electron transport chain running, so NAD+ must be regenerated another way
quiz.why: Converting pyruvate to lactate recycles NADH back to NAD+ so glycolysis can continue producing 2 ATP per glucose. Glucose supply and mitochondrial integrity are not the limiting factors.

quiz.q: Where does the citric acid cycle take place, and what is its main output?
choices: Mitochondrial matrix; NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain
quiz.why: The cycle runs in the matrix and its chief product is reduced electron carriers, which power oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis is the cytosolic step yielding 2 ATP.

quiz.q: A patient in prolonged starvation has ketone bodies in the blood. These come from:
choices: Hepatic conversion of surplus acetyl CoA when carbohydrate is scarce
quiz.why: With carbohydrate gone, fat is mobilized and the liver turns excess acetyl CoA into ketones the brain can use. Glycogen is exhausted long before ketosis develops.

quiz.q: A febrile patient shivers while their temperature climbs from 37 C to 39 C. The reason is:
choices: The hypothalamic set point has been raised, so 37 C now reads as too cold
quiz.why: Pyrogens reset the thermostat upward, so the body actively generates heat to reach the new target. Failure of heat loss with a normal set point describes heat stroke instead.

quiz.q: Which structures form the filtration membrane of the nephron?
choices: Loop of Henle and vasa recta
quiz.why: Filtration occurs only at the renal corpuscle, where glomerular capillaries sit inside Bowman capsule. The other pairs are reabsorption or transport structures.

quiz.q: Severe hemorrhage drops renal perfusion. Which combination of responses is expected?
choices: Renin release, angiotensin II formation, aldosterone secretion, water and sodium retention
Afferent arteriole dilation with increased GFR
quiz.why: Low perfusion activates RAAS to restore volume and pressure. ANP release and reduced ADH are responses to volume overload, the opposite situation.

quiz.q: Which part of the nephron reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtrate?
quiz.why: The PCT reclaims all glucose and amino acids plus about 65% of sodium and water. The distal segments perform hormone-controlled fine tuning of much smaller volumes.

quiz.q: A patient with severe vomiting for two days presents with pH 7.52. The most likely disorder is:
choices: Metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid
quiz.why: Vomiting removes hydrochloric acid, leaving a relative bicarbonate excess. A respiratory cause would show an abnormal CO2 as the primary driver instead.

quiz.q: Which hormone maintains the corpus luteum during early pregnancy?
choices: Human chorionic gonadotropin from the trophoblast
quiz.why: hCG from the developing embryo prevents luteal regression so progesterone continues and the endometrium is preserved. Pituitary LH falls once pregnancy is established.

quiz.q: The surge that triggers ovulation is caused by:
choices: Sustained high estrogen switching feedback from negative to positive, causing an LH surge
Rising FSH from the corpus luteum
quiz.why: Mature follicle estrogen reaches a threshold that flips the pituitary response to positive feedback, producing the LH spike. The corpus luteum forms after ovulation, not before.

quiz.q: A father is color blind (X-linked recessive) and the mother is not a carrier. What is true of their children?
choices: All sons will be color blind
All daughters will be carriers, and no sons will be affected
Half the daughters will be affected
No child can inherit the allele
quiz.why: The father passes his affected X to every daughter, making them carriers, and passes his Y to every son. Sons receive their only X from the unaffected, non-carrier mother.

quiz.q: Which germ layer gives rise to the nervous system and the epidermis?
quiz.why: Ectoderm forms outer coverings and neural tissue. Mesoderm forms muscle, bone and blood; endoderm forms gut and glandular linings.

scenarios.title: Exam walkthrough: tracing a drop of blood and a molecule of oxygen
scenarios.intro: The cardiopulmonary unit exam ends with a chained tracing question worth 25 points: *Follow a red blood cell from the right atrium until it delivers oxygen to a working quadriceps muscle, naming every chamber, valve and vessel, and explain what makes the oxygen let go at the tissue.* Partial credit is given per named structure, and reversals cost points. Work it in order.

steps.prompt: Your red cell is in the **right atrium**, arriving from the superior vena cava. Where does it go next, and through what?

choices.text: Through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle
choices.feedback: Correct. Right side is tricuspid, left side is bicuspid or mitral. Naming the valve, not just the chamber, is where the point lives.

choices.text: Through the mitral valve into the right ventricle
choices.feedback: Right chamber, wrong valve. The mitral valve is on the left side. Sides get swapped constantly on this question.

choices.text: Through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery
choices.feedback: You skipped the right ventricle entirely. Blood must pass a ventricle before it can enter an artery.

choices.text: Through the foramen ovale into the left atrium
choices.feedback: That is the fetal shunt, which closes at birth. In an adult it does not exist as a functional pathway.

steps.prompt: The cell is in the **right ventricle**. Trace it to the point where it actually picks up oxygen.

choices.text: Pulmonary valve, pulmonary trunk and arteries, pulmonary capillaries around the alveoli
choices.feedback: Correct. Note the exception worth naming for credit: the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood, the only arteries that do.

choices.text: Aortic valve, aorta, bronchial arteries
choices.feedback: The bronchial arteries feed lung tissue itself, they do not participate in gas exchange. And the right ventricle never opens into the aorta.

choices.text: Pulmonary valve, pulmonary veins, alveolar capillaries
choices.feedback: Order error. The veins are the return path from the lung, not the delivery path to it.

steps.prompt: At the alveolus, oxygen must cross into the cell. Which explanation earns full credit for the mechanism?

choices.text: Active transport of oxygen across the respiratory membrane using ATP
choices.feedback: Gas exchange is entirely passive. Alveolar cells spend no ATP moving oxygen, and calling it active transport is a hard error.

choices.text: Simple diffusion down a partial pressure gradient, alveolar PO2 about 104 mmHg versus arriving blood about 40 mmHg, across a 0.5 micrometer membrane
choices.feedback: Correct and complete. Naming both partial pressures and the membrane's thinness is what separates full credit from half.

choices.text: Diffusion down a gradient
choices.feedback: The mechanism is right but bare. Tracing prompts want the numbers — 104 and 40 mmHg — because they prove you know which direction the gradient points.

steps.prompt: The oxygenated cell returns to the heart. Trace it from the lung to the quadriceps.

choices.text: Pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, common iliac, external iliac, femoral artery, muscle capillaries
choices.feedback: Correct, and the arterial naming in the lower limb is exactly the part most students skip. Abdominal aorta to common iliac to external iliac to femoral is the chain.

choices.text: Pulmonary arteries, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aorta, femoral artery
choices.feedback: The return from the lung is by pulmonary veins. Arteries carry blood away from the heart by definition, even when the blood inside them is deoxygenated.

choices.text: Pulmonary veins, left atrium, tricuspid valve, left ventricle, aorta, femoral artery
choices.feedback: Side swap again. The left atrioventricular valve is the bicuspid or mitral valve; tricuspid is on the right.

steps.prompt: Final part: **why does oxygen let go at the exercising muscle** but not in the resting forearm the cell passed on the way? Choose the fullest answer.

choices.text: Because hemoglobin is used up after one pass
choices.feedback: Hemoglobin is not consumed. It unloads and reloads continuously for the red cell's entire 120-day life.

choices.text: Working muscle is warm, acidic and CO2-rich, which shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin curve right and lowers hemoglobin's affinity — the Bohr effect — while the low tissue PO2 steepens the gradient
choices.feedback: Correct and complete. The curve shift plus the low tissue partial pressure are two separate mechanisms and both earn points.

choices.text: Because tissue PO2 is lower there
choices.feedback: True and worth partial credit, but incomplete. Without naming the rightward curve shift and its causes you lose the physiology half of the answer.

scenarios.debrief: Chained tracing questions test three separate skills at once and are graded on all three. First, sequence: chamber, valve, vessel, in strict order, with no skipped steps. Second, laterality: tricuspid right, mitral left, and the pulmonary vessels as the one place where artery does not mean oxygenated. Third, mechanism with numbers: alveolar PO2 104 versus venous 40, a 0.5 micrometer membrane, and a rightward Bohr shift from heat, acid and CO2. Write the trace as a numbered list and the mechanism as prose underneath. Students who write only prose lose sequencing points they actually earned.

scenarios.title: Case reasoning: the polyuria question on the final
scenarios.intro: Your instructor puts a case on the board for the cumulative final. *A 22-year-old reports urinating enormous volumes and being constantly thirsty for three weeks. Urine output is roughly 6 L/day.* You will be asked to narrow it, name the hormone or transport step responsible, and predict the lab. Reason with the mechanisms, not with memorized disease names.

steps.prompt: You get one lab test before committing. Which single result narrows the differential most?

choices.text: Serum glucose
choices.feedback: Correct. Polyuria has two big mechanisms on this syllabus — an osmotic diuresis from glucose exceeding the renal threshold, or a water-handling failure from ADH. Glucose separates them in one test.

choices.text: Serum calcium
choices.feedback: Hypercalcemia can cause polyuria, but it is far down the list and does not split the two main mechanisms you were taught.

choices.text: Hemoglobin and hematocrit
choices.feedback: This tells you about red cell mass, not water handling. It would not change your reasoning at all here.

choices.text: Arterial blood gas
choices.feedback: Useful later if ketoacidosis is confirmed, but it does not identify why the patient is making 6 L of urine.

steps.prompt: Serum glucose comes back at `92 mg/dL` — normal. Urine specific gravity is very low and urine osmolality is about `80 mOsm/kg`. What does this tell you?

choices.text: The kidney is failing to concentrate urine, pointing to an ADH problem rather than an osmotic diuresis
choices.feedback: Correct. Normal glucose rules out osmotic diuresis. Urine this dilute means the collecting duct is not reabsorbing water — diabetes insipidus, not mellitus.

choices.text: The patient has diabetes mellitus with a normal fasting glucose
choices.feedback: You cannot have glycosuric osmotic diuresis without glucose above the renal threshold of about 180 mg/dL. Normal glucose closes that door.

choices.text: Aldosterone is excessive
choices.feedback: Aldosterone excess retains sodium and water, so it would reduce urine output, not increase it, and would show hypokalemia rather than dilute polyuria.

steps.prompt: Name the precise transport step that has failed, the part the grader is looking for.

choices.text: The loop of Henle has stopped building the medullary gradient
choices.feedback: Possible in theory, but ADH deficiency is far more common and the gradient itself is usually intact. This answer misses the hormone entirely.

choices.text: Without ADH, aquaporins are not inserted into the collecting duct, so water cannot follow the medullary osmotic gradient out of the filtrate
choices.feedback: Correct, and this is the full-credit sentence: name the hormone, the channel, the segment, and the gradient it would have used.

choices.text: The proximal convoluted tubule stops reabsorbing sodium
choices.feedback: That would cause massive electrolyte loss and volume collapse, not isolated dilute polyuria with normal electrolytes.

steps.prompt: The instructor extends the case: *the patient stops drinking for eight hours as a test.* Predict what happens to serum sodium and to urine osmolality.

choices.text: Serum sodium rises and urine stays dilute, because water loss continues regardless of intake
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the water deprivation test in one sentence — free water keeps leaving, so plasma concentrates while urine stays inappropriately dilute.

choices.text: Serum sodium falls and urine concentrates normally
choices.feedback: That is the healthy response. If the patient could concentrate urine on deprivation, ADH would be working and the diagnosis would be wrong.

choices.text: Both stay unchanged because the kidney compensates
choices.feedback: There is no compensation available. Without ADH the collecting duct is simply impermeable to water no matter how dehydrated the patient becomes.

steps.prompt: Last part, worth five points: *contrast this condition with the one whose name it shares.*

choices.text: Both are ADH disorders; one affects the kidney and one the pituitary
choices.feedback: Only half true. Diabetes insipidus does come in central and nephrogenic forms, but the condition being contrasted is diabetes mellitus, which has nothing to do with ADH.

choices.text: Diabetes insipidus is a water problem from absent or ineffective ADH with normal glucose. Diabetes mellitus is a glucose problem from absent or ineffective insulin, causing osmotic diuresis once glucose exceeds about 180 mg/dL
choices.feedback: Correct. Naming the renal threshold is what turns a definition into an explanation of why mellitus also causes polyuria.

choices.text: They are the same disease at different severities
choices.feedback: They share only the word diabetes, which means to pass through. The mechanisms, labs and treatments have nothing in common.

scenarios.debrief: Physiology cases are solved by asking which transport step could produce the finding, not by pattern-matching a disease name. Polyuria has exactly two mechanisms on this syllabus: solute dragging water out (glucose above the roughly 180 mg/dL renal threshold) or water failing to be reabsorbed (no ADH, no aquaporins in the collecting duct). One glucose level splits them. Then say the full sentence the grader wants — hormone, channel, tubule segment, and the gradient involved. The same reasoning chain handles edema (hydrostatic versus oncotic versus lymphatic) and acid-base (respiratory versus metabolic, primary versus compensation).
